content.title: Which metric would you track to most effectively evaluate the inclusivity of a transport electrification initiative?

options.value: Number of low-income individuals adopting electric mobility options
Percentage of public transportation fleet electrified in underserved areas
Average income level of households using new electric transport modes
Rate of participation from marginalized communities in planning processes

takeaways.title: Transport Emissions Demand Urgent Reduction Efforts.
takeaways.description: Transport accounts for over one-third of CO₂ emissions from end-use sectors, with emissions rising 3% in 2022 alone. To meet global climate goals, transport emissions must decline by over 3% annually until 2030, necessitating a shift toward cleaner energy sources, efficiency improvements, and policies promoting low-carbon mobility.

takeaways.title: Electrification is Key to Reducing Road Transport Emissions.
takeaways.description: Road transport is the largest contributor to transport emissions, making vehicle electrification a key solution. EV adoption is growing rapidly, with electric cars expected to make up nearly 50% of the global auto market by 2030. In developing countries, focusing on shared electric mobility, such as e-buses, two- and three-wheelers, can improve accessibility, cut costs, and support a just energy transition.

takeaways.title: Overcoming Key Challenges to Unlock Electrification’s Full Potential.
takeaways.description: Challenges such as high upfront costs, limited charging infrastructure, and increased demand for critical minerals must be addressed through targeted policies, innovative financing, and circular economy solutions like battery recycling. Ensuring local value addition in mineral-rich countries and preparing the workforce for new job opportunities are crucial to making transport electrification both sustainable and equitable.

content.text:
The buildings sector, which includes construction, heating, cooling, lighting, and appliances, accounts for over one-third of global energy consumption and emissions. Operations alone are responsible for 30% of global final energy use and 26% of energy-related emissions, with 8% from direct emissions and 18% from indirect emissions tied to electricity and heat production.
While direct emissions slightly decreased to 3 Gt in 2022, indirect emissions rose to nearly 6.8 Gt due to increased reliance on electricity. Despite some progress, the sector remains off-track to meet the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (NZE) Scenario. Addressing this requires a concerted effort to improve energy efficiency 💬️ and adopt renewable energy technologies.

While the ASI framework provides the strategic direction, technical tools like energy auditing are necessary for operationalizing the "Improve" pillar. The Republic of Moldova's initiative to train energy auditors specifically for the transport sector is a model for other LMICs.21
Energy auditing in transport involves a comprehensive evaluation of fuel consumption factors, ranging from vehicle technical condition and fuel type to infrastructure quality and even car body color.21 By understanding these variables in an integrated manner, auditors can identify high-impact interventions that reduce final energy consumption—which, in Moldova's case, is 30% for transport.21 This data-driven approach is essential for ensuring that limited public and private resources are invested where they will yield the greatest energy savings and emission reductions.

The Improve Pillar: Optimizing Vehicle and Fuel Technology

The "Improve" pillar focuses on the technological optimization of vehicles and fuels to reduce their environmental footprint. This includes enhancing the energy efficiency of internal combustion engines, transitioning to electric mobility 💬️, and integrating renewable energy into the transport power mix.1While Improve strategies are essential, they are often over-relied upon in National Determined Contributions (NDCs), accounting for 52% of all planned measures globally.
Technological improvements must be coupled with rigorous standards. For example, Moldova has recently launched its first professional training program for energy auditing in the transport sector, recognizing that auditing is the first step toward optimizing fleet consumption and reducing the 30% share of final energy consumption held by transport in the country.

For electric vehicles, the Improve pillar also encompasses the decarbonization of the electricity grid; an electric two-wheeler in a coal-heavy grid like India's currently has a higher lifecycle emission profile than one in Vietnam, where natural gas and renewables play a larger role.

The Shift Pillar: Promoting Energy-Efficient Modes

The "Shift" pillar seeks to improve the efficiency of individual trips by moving travelers from energy-intensive modes, such as private cars, to more environmentally friendly options like public transport, walking, and cycling. In many developing nations, the challenge is not just to shift passengers to these modes but to maintain the already high share of public and non-motorized transport in the face of rising incomes.

Public transport systems, such as Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) and rail, are the backbones of the Shift strategy. BRT, pioneered in cities like Curitiba and Bogotá, offers rail-like quality and capacity at a fraction of the cost, making it particularly suitable for the budget constraints of developing cities. Furthermore, active mobility, walking and cycling, represents the most energy-efficient form of transport. Successful implementation requires the reallocation of road space to dedicated bike lanes and widened sidewalks, as seen in the "Cycling Capital" of Lviv, Ukraine, where significant progress was achieved in just three years.

The Avoid Pillar: Reducing the Need for Motorized Travel

The primary objective of the "Avoid" pillar is to improve the efficiency of the transport system by reducing the need for motorized travel and shortening trip lengths. This is fundamentally an exercise in integrated land-use planning. By promoting high-density, compact urban development, cities can ensure that daily needs, such as groceries, schools, and workplaces, are within walking or cycling distance of residential areas.

A critical component of the Avoid strategy is Transit-Oriented Development (TOD), which concentrates commercial and residential density around high-capacity public transport hubs.. This reduces the "last-mile" distance and incentivizes residents to forgo private vehicle ownership. In the context of developing cities, fine-grained urban fabric where small-scale retail is permitted on the ground floors of residential buildings serves as a natural Avoid mechanism. Digitalization also plays an increasing role in the Avoid pillar, as teleworking and e-governance reduce the need for physical commutes.

This framework has guided sustainable transport strategies for over a decade, providing a hierarchy of interventions that prioritizes human-centered planning over technology-centric fixes. The ASI approach moves away from the traditional "predict-provide-manage" model, which often results in induced demand for private vehicle travel, toward a model that seeks to manage mobility demand as a finite resource.

1: Road Transport
Road transport is by far the largest component of transport-related emissions. In Europe, it accounted for approximately 74% of total transport emissions in 2023, with passenger cars alone responsible for more than half of these. Globally, road transport passenger and freight emissions represented 69% of all transport emissions in 2019, reaching 6.1 GtCO2-eq.

Trends in road transport emissions are influenced by increasing demand for travel, population growth, economic growth, and urban sprawl, which have led to a 47% increase in vehicle miles traveled (VMT) by light-duty motor vehicles between 1990 and 2022. While there has been a trend towards larger, less fuel-efficient vehicles, average new vehicle fuel economy has improved almost every year since 2005, helping to slow the rate of CO2 emission increases. Despite these efficiency gains, the slow turnover of the global vehicle fleet means that gasoline vehicles continue to dominate, limiting the immediate impact of new, cleaner technologies.

The nexus between energy and transport in the Global South is defined by a unique set of constraints and opportunities. While high-income countries are primarily concerned with replacing an established fleet of private internal combustion engine vehicles with electric alternatives, developing nations face the challenge of building sustainable mobility systems from the ground up during a period of unprecedented demographic growth. For these nations, transport energy sustainability is inextricably linked to energy security, as many are net importers of fossil fuels, leaving them vulnerable to global price volatility.

The economic burden of inefficient transport is profound. In Vietnam, for instance, the World Bank estimates that urban air pollution, largely attributed to traffic concentration, costs the economy approximately $10 billion annually in health-related expenses. Furthermore, the lack of reliable public transport often forces the poorest citizens to reside in peripheral areas with limited access to job centers, creating a cycle of poverty reinforced by "mobility poverty". UNDP's integrated approach, facilitated through the Sustainable Energy Hub, seeks to drive systemic transformation by linking policy, technology, and finance to ensure that no one is left behind in the transition to low-carbon mobility.

The transport sector is a major contributor to global greenhouse gas emissions, predominantly relying on fossil fuels. Decarbonizing this sector is a complex challenge, requiring a multi-pronged approach involving electrification, fuel efficiency improvements, and the adoption of alternative fuels.

Transport, specifically, is responsible for nearly a quarter of energy-related global greenhouse gas emissions, with road traffic alone contributing 70% of that total. In developing countries and emerging economies, transport demand is growing at an exponential rate, driven by rapid urbanization and a rising middle class that increasingly views private vehicle ownership as the only viable means of mobility. Without ambitious policy intervention, transport-related CO2 emissions could grow by 16% to 50% by the year 2050.

2: Shipping
International shipping relies heavily on oil-based fuels, which historically constitute over 99% of its total energy demand. In 2022, CO2 emissions from international shipping grew by 5%, accounting for approximately 2% of global energy-related CO2 emissions. Oil tankers alone contribute about 13% of maritime emissions, equating to approximately 114 million tons of CO2. Beyond CO2, the combustion of fossil fuels for water-borne navigation also produces methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), carbon monoxide (CO), oxides of nitrogen (NOx), non-methane volatile organic compounds (NMVOCs), and sulfur dioxide (SO2). The amount of emissions is primarily a function of fuel consumed, fuel characteristics, engine technology, and emission controls. While cargo vessels are highly efficient per unit of payload, international waters have historically operated under less stringent pollution regulations, though new UN regulations are coming into effect.

3: Aviation
Aviation accounts for a relatively small share of global emissions but is one of the most challenging sectors to decarbonize due to the high energy density requirements of air travel. In 2023, aviation was responsible for 2.5% of global energy-related CO2 emissions, having grown faster than rail, road, or shipping between 2000 and 2019. As international travel rebounded from COVID-19 pandemic lows, aviation emissions reached almost 950 Mt CO2 in 2023, exceeding 90% of pre-pandemic levels.
Technological improvements in airframe and engine design, along with operational optimizations such as higher passenger load factors, have led to significant energy efficiency gains. For instance, the energy required to travel one passenger-kilometer more than halved between 1990 and 2019. However, the carbon intensity of jet fuel itself has remained unchanged, meaning that while flying has become more energy-efficient, the fuel burned is no cleaner. This highlights the need for a fundamental shift away from conventional jet fuel to achieve substantial emissions reductions in aviation.
